note: Search titles (without the ' · Money Research' suffix, max 70 characters) and descriptions (max 160 characters, never truncated) for chapter pages. Each restates the chapter's own content or approved short answer; qualifications stay in.

gold-01.title: Why gold? The metal's properties and the earliest gold finds
gold-01.description: Why gold became special: durable, workable and sometimes found as native metal. The Varna finds are early evidence, but properties alone didn't make it money.

gold-02.title: Before money: gold as ornament, ritual and royal treasure
gold-02.description: Before coins, gold served as ornament, ritual object, royal treasure and diplomatic gift, and in some societies as weighed metal for payment.

gold-03.title: From weighed metal to the first coins: how gold became money
gold-03.description: How weighed metal became stamped coin: a stamp named the issuer and denomination and eased checking, but a coin's value still depended on acceptance.

gold-04.title: What gives gold its value, and when it became a unit of account
gold-04.description: Why gold has value: physical uses and monetary properties matter, but its price also reflects social acceptance, institutions, expectations and markets.

gold-05.title: Silver, copper, bronze and bimetallism: gold's rival metals
gold-05.description: Was money always backed by gold? No. Silver, copper and bronze were coins, account units or tokens; a mint ratio was not a promise to redeem in gold.

gold-06.title: How empires used gold: coins, treasuries, gifts and wealth
gold-06.description: How empires used gold for coins, treasuries, gifts and wealth, while silver, copper, paper and credit often handled accounting and everyday payments.

gold-07.title: The gold standard, 1717–1971: how it worked and why it ended
gold-07.description: Why the gold standard ended: Britain's 1931 sterling crisis, the US suspension of domestic gold conversion in 1933, and Nixon's 1971 gold-window closure.

gold-08.title: Why the dollar replaced gold and outlived gold convertibility
gold-08.description: Why the dollar kept its role after gold: reserve, trade, banking and securities uses. Oil invoicing helped, but no reviewed 1974 document shows oil redemption.

gold-09.title: Gold today (2026): prices, reserves and what still holds value
gold-09.description: Gold in 2026: what World Gold Council, ECB and IMF data show on prices, flows and reserve shares, and why they don't guarantee gold works as a hedge.

after-01.title: The Nixon shock, 1971: the end of dollar–gold convertibility
after-01.description: On 15 August 1971 Nixon closed the gold window. Major currencies floated later, and the IMF's Second Amendment took effect in 1978: three separate steps.

after-02.title: Oil shocks, petrodollars and stagflation, 1973–1982
after-02.description: 1970s stagflation: oil shocks intensified an inflation already under way. Petrodollars meant dollar invoicing and recycling, not redeeming dollars for oil.

after-03.title: The 1980s debt crisis, the Brady plan and the managed dollar
after-03.description: The 1980s debt crisis: high dollar interest rates and weak export earnings strained borrowers, then came workouts, Brady restructuring and Basel capital rules.

after-04.title: After the Cold War: new nations, new currencies and the euro
after-04.description: After the Cold War, new states chose different currencies, pegs and frameworks. Yugoslavia's January 1994 hyperinflation was an extreme case, not the rule.

after-05.title: Emerging-market currency crises, 1990–2001
after-05.description: The 1990s emerging-market crises: pegs and short-term foreign borrowing left economies exposed to capital outflows, but no single mechanism explains them.

after-06.title: War and money, 1971–2026: borrowing, energy and asset freezes
after-06.description: How war affects money: public borrowing, energy prices and access to financial claims. Effects vary by conflict; an asset freeze does not transfer ownership.

after-07.title: The 2008 financial crisis and quantitative easing (QE), 2007–2019
after-07.description: The 2008 crisis: housing-credit losses, leverage and fragile funding, and how rate cuts, emergency lending, dollar swaps and QE differed as responses.

after-08.title: How money went digital: cards, Bitcoin, stablecoins and CBDCs
after-08.description: How money went digital, 1971–2026: cards, payment rails, Bitcoin, stablecoins and CBDCs, and why faster messaging is not faster final payment.

after-09.title: Pandemic inflation and weaponised reserves, 2020–2026
after-09.description: 2020s inflation: pandemic spending, central-bank buying, supply shocks and rate rises; 2022 limits on Russia's reserves; gold's share rising through valuation.

after-10.title: Rules of the fiat era: the IMF, central banks and Basel
after-10.description: Who sets the rules of fiat money: IMF agreements, national law, central banks and bank-supervision standards, each with different mandates since 1971.

bitcoin-01.title: Bitcoin's origin: what the 2008 financial crisis produced
bitcoin-01.description: Bitcoin's origin: after the 2008 crisis it let anyone verify issuance and transfers without a central ledger operator. Exchanges and custodians grew around it.

bitcoin-02.title: What Bitcoin solved, and what it did not
bitcoin-02.description: What Bitcoin solved: self-custody and independent validation cut reliance on account providers. What it didn't: confirmation, access, custody and price risk.

bitcoin-03.title: How Bitcoin is actually used: global adoption, 2009–2026
bitcoin-03.description: How Bitcoin is used: investment, custody and some payments, and why surveys, exchange data, on-chain flows and Lightning capacity measure different things.

bitcoin-04.title: Bitcoin as legal tender: El Salvador, the CAR and what happened
bitcoin-04.description: El Salvador's 2021 Bitcoin law and 2025 rollback, the Central African Republic, and why holding or mining Bitcoin doesn't make it a national pricing unit.

bitcoin-05.title: The Bitcoin standard debate: who supports it, who opposes it
bitcoin-05.description: The Bitcoin standard debate: officials, staff authors, policy papers and an executive order carry different authority and address different proposed uses.

bitcoin-06.title: Is Bitcoin legal tender? What legal tender really requires
bitcoin-06.description: Does legal tender make Bitcoin a unit of account? No. Debt rules, taxes, private acceptance, prices and reserves depend on each country's law and use.

bitcoin-07.title: Bitcoin's fixed supply: could it be the unit of an economy?
bitcoin-07.description: Does a fixed Bitcoin base fix the whole money supply? No. Deposits, lending, velocity and prices depend on the banking system built around it.

bitcoin-08.title: Bitcoin vs gold as a reserve asset: why not gold again?
bitcoin-08.description: Bitcoin vs gold as a reserve asset: compare law, custody, liquidity, loss horizon and mandate, using the same dates and units for performance claims.

bitcoin-09.title: Who controls Bitcoin? Holders, miners, validators and custodians
bitcoin-09.description: Who controls Bitcoin: validators enforce their chosen rules, while miners, custodians, key holders, exchanges and the law affect different steps of using it.

bitcoin-10.title: A Bitcoin reserve or standard for the US, China, Europe and others?
bitcoin-10.description: Could large economies move to a Bitcoin reserve or standard? Private access, public investment, reserves and native pricing are separate decisions.

bitcoin-11.title: Why Bitcoin hasn't become a global currency
bitcoin-11.description: Why Bitcoin isn't a global currency: fixed issuance is a design constraint; payment use, price stability, credit and custody must be measured in practice.

bitcoin-12.title: Could Bitcoin reproduce old financial crises and bank runs?
bitcoin-12.description: Could Bitcoin repeat old crises? Custodians, leverage and redeemable claims can spread run or forced-sale risk, but analogies don't prove identical crises.

bitcoin-13.title: Is Bitcoin the answer to money after gold?
bitcoin-13.description: Is Bitcoin the answer after gold? It eases some issuer and intermediary trust problems; wide use as a pricing unit or a reliable hedge is not established.

zcash-01.title: From gold, fiat and Bitcoin to Zcash: the lessons that carry over
zcash-01.description: What the history of gold, fiat and Bitcoin teaches about Zcash: which lessons carry over to private digital money, and which earlier claims need qualifying.

zcash-02.title: What is Zcash? How shielded payments work and what is live
zcash-02.description: What is Zcash? A public network whose shielded payments can be verified without revealing sender, recipient or amount, and what is actually live in 2026.

zcash-03.title: Which world problems can Zcash address?
zcash-03.description: Which problems Zcash can reduce, which it inherits or worsens, and which it leaves untouched: a problem-by-problem look at private digital cash.

zcash-04.title: Privacy and fungibility: the distinctive case for Zcash
zcash-04.description: Why privacy and fungibility matter for money, how Zcash's shielded payments support them, and how unique that case really is.

zcash-05.title: Can ZEC be a unit of account? What a ZEC economy would need
zcash-05.description: Can ZEC be a unit of account? What would count as a ZEC economy, with prices, wages, debts and taxes set in ZEC, and whether one is possible.

zcash-06.title: Zcash's fixed supply: credit, banks and crisis management
zcash-06.description: What a fixed ZEC supply would mean for inflation, lending, banks and emergency liquidity when no one can create unlimited base ZEC in a crisis.

zcash-07.title: Zcash adoption: legal, commercial and institutional barriers
zcash-07.description: The legal, commercial and institutional obstacles to Zcash adoption within today's financial and legal system.

zcash-08.title: Gold → fiat → Bitcoin → Zcash: transition or analogy?
zcash-08.description: Gold, fiat, Bitcoin, Zcash: what the sequence means, whether it is a real transition or only an analogy, and where the analogy fails.

zcash-09.title: Zcash risks: cryptography, governance, mining and upgrades
zcash-09.description: Zcash-specific risks: what could fail in its cryptography, governance, mining, wallets and future network upgrades.

zcash-10.title: A world ready for ZEC? A hypothesis and how to test it
zcash-10.description: A thought experiment: what system could support pricing in ZEC, how it might be adopted, how it would handle stress, and what evidence would reject it.
